name: subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn
aliases: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn
subcutaneous fat necrosis of the neonate
subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn

clinicalPearls: A self-limiting lobular panniculitis of term and post-term neonates, typically appearing in the first days to weeks of life as firm, indurated, red-violaceous nodules and plaques.
Characteristic sites are areas rich in fat and subject to pressure: the back, buttocks, shoulders, cheeks and proximal limbs.
Risk factors include perinatal asphyxia, hypothermia (including therapeutic cooling), meconium aspiration, pre-eclampsia and maternal factors such as gestational diabetes.
The infant is usually otherwise well, in contrast to sclerema neonatorum which affects sick, premature neonates diffusely.
The principal and potentially life-threatening complication is hypercalcaemia, which may be delayed for weeks after the skin lesions appear.
Histology shows fat necrosis with a granulomatous infiltrate and pathognomonic needle-shaped clefts (radial crystals of triglyceride) within adipocytes and giant cells.
Other metabolic derangements include thrombocytopenia, hypertriglyceridaemia and hypoglycaemia, warranting monitoring.
Skin lesions resolve spontaneously over weeks to months, but serum calcium must be monitored well beyond cutaneous resolution.
reference.pathophysiology: Neonatal subcutaneous fat has a high ratio of saturated (stearic and palmitic) to unsaturated fatty acids and a higher melting point than adult fat, predisposing it to crystallise and solidify under stress. Perinatal hypoxia, hypothermia and local pressure cause ischaemic injury to this metabolically vulnerable fat, triggering crystallisation and necrosis of adipocytes with liberation of fatty acids. A granulomatous inflammatory response ensues, with foreign-body giant cells containing characteristic radially arranged needle-shaped crystal clefts. The associated hypercalcaemia is attributed largely to extrarenal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity within the granulomatous infiltrate producing 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, augmented by prostaglandin E and release of calcium from necrotic fat.
additionalDifferentials: bacillus Calmette-Guerin or other iatrogenic injection-site reactions
congenital infantile haemangioma or other vascular tumours
poststeroid panniculitis (in infants weaned off corticosteroids)
additionalInvestigations: serial serum calcium (including ionised calcium) for several weeks to months
serum phosphate, magnesium, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D metabolites
skin biopsy for histopathology when diagnosis is uncertain (needle-shaped clefts, granulomatous panniculitis)
renal ultrasound and urinary calcium if nephrocalcinosis is suspected
electrocardiogram if significant hypercalcaemia is detected
redFlags: hypercalcaemia causing irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy or seizures
nephrocalcinosis or renal impairment from sustained hypercalcaemia
extensive or ulcerating lesions predisposing to secondary infection
cardiac arrhythmia associated with severe hypercalcaemia
systemically unwell infant suggesting sclerema neonatorum or sepsis rather than isolated fat necrosis
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution over weeks to months, but the outcome hinges on detecting and managing hypercalcaemia, which can be delayed and, if unrecognised, cause metastatic calcification or renal damage.
pitfalls: Discharging the infant once skin lesions improve without arranging prolonged calcium monitoring.
Confusing it with sclerema neonatorum, which carries a far graver prognosis and different clinical context.
Attributing hypercalcaemic symptoms to feeding difficulties or sepsis.
Failing to recognise therapeutic hypothermia as a precipitating factor.
Overlooking thrombocytopenia or hypertriglyceridaemia in the metabolic work-up.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Textbook of Neonatal Dermatology, current edition
management: Treat conservatively as a self-limiting panniculitis, with supportive skin care while the nodules involute spontaneously
Perform serial serum calcium monitoring for several weeks to months, since hypercalcaemia is often delayed and potentially life-threatening
Manage symptomatic hypercalcaemia with hyperhydration using intravenous fluids and a loop diuretic to promote calciuresis
Add corticosteroids to suppress extrarenal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, escalating to calcitonin or a bisphosphonate if refractory
Limit dietary calcium and vitamin D and avoid supplements during the vulnerable period
Monitor renal function with renal ultrasound and urinary calcium for nephrocalcinosis, and check platelet count, glucose and triglycerides
Optimise perinatal care with correction of hypoxia and hypothermia, and involve neonatal and paediatric endocrine teams
